titleStmt.title: Minimizing the Response Times of Aperiodic Tasks in Hard Real-time Systems with EDF

analytic.title: Minimizing the Response Times of Aperiodic Tasks in Hard Real-time Systems with EDF

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper presents a new aperiodic request server in a hard real-time system handling periodic and aperiodic tasks, using EDF (Earliest deadline first) in order to schedule periodic tasks. The objective of the server is to reduce response times for aperiodic tasks and guaranteeing the schedulability of all periodic tasks (considered as critical tasks). This server improves the response time offered by TBS (Total Bandwidth Server), because idle times, aperiodic and periodic tasks are considered for deadline assignment. The optimality of the server is also proved. Finally a performance evaluation is made by comparing the server with TBS in different periodic and aperiodic load levels.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: A real-time system demands that its results be both logically correct and delivered on time. In fact, realtime applications need to execute many processes or tasks with timing, precedence and resource constraints. However, a real-time system is characterized by a timing constraint called deadline, which represents the time before a process should complete its execution without causing any damage to the system.

Depending on the consequences caused by a missed deadline, real-time tasks are usually classified in [2]: Hard (a missed deadline causes catastrophic consequences in the system) and Soft (a missed deadline decreases system performance). A system is considered to be a hard real-time system, if a failure caused by a missed deadline may lead to disastrous effects.

Hence, generating a plan for satisfying task constraints is much important. This plan is called schedule, and it is created by the tasks scheduler. In order to make a schedule, the scheduler uses a predefined criterion known as scheduling policy. In this way, the set of rules that, at any time, determines the order in which tasks are executed is called a scheduling algorithm.

Nevertheless, scheduling may become a NPcomplete problem [7], because of the task constraints. For instance, a task can be defined as a periodic or an aperiodic task. Periodic tasks consist of an infinite sequence of identical activities, called instances or jobs that are regularly activated at a constant rate. On the other hand, aperiodic tasks also consist of an infinite sequence of identical instances, however, their activation times are not regular.
Thus, scheduling is the mixed activity of processor (or processors) and resources assigning to each task in the system, in order to complete their time-constrained computation [1].

This paper presents a new way to adapt aperiodic tasks (called server or task to service to aperiodic tasks [9]) to be implemented in a hard real-time system where periodic tasks are scheduled by EDF (Earliest Deadline First) [8].

The proposal presented tries to give optimal response times in the aperiodic tasks but keeping the schedulability in the periodic tasks in a real-time environment, where the aperiodic tasks are attended in a FIFO order.
It is similar to TBS [10] and ITBS [6], but it considers other aspects for improving response times in the aperiodic tasks.

The paper is organized as follows: First, it gives the system model where the proposed server is based on. In the next section, describes a new server to improve the response time of soft aperiodic tasks, then it presents the performance results generated by the TBS, and the proposed server (MDAS). Finally, conclusions are presented.

div.head: Assumptions
div.p: A single-processor system which has a set of soft aperiodic task and a set of periodic task . Each periodic task i has a period T i , a computation time C i , and a relative deadline D i equal to its period. Periodic tasks are scheduled using dynamicpriority assignment, namely Earliest Deadline First (EDF); All periodic tasks start simultaneously at time t=0. Arrival times of aperiodic requests are unknown but their computation times are known once they arrive When there is no explicitly specified arrival time, the minimum interarrival time of a sporadic task is assumed to be equal to its deadline. The tasks are preemptive (i.e. they may be suspended and inserted into the ready queue to service ready tasks with major priority). All periodic tasks have hard deadlines. All aperiodic tasks do not have deadlines.

div.head: Minimum Deadline Assignment Server ( MDAS )
div.p: This section shows a new server to assign the minimum deadline to each aperiodic task, considering idle times, and assuming the assignment is still done when there is one or more aperiodic task to execute. In order to consider these issues, the server takes into account a similar concept to Baruah´s processor demand [3] to verify and maintain the schedulability, it is the "processor real demand (H(t))".

For verifying the schedulability, Baruah [4][3] proposes next theorem: the schedulability of a periodic task set is guaranteed if and only if the cumulative processor demand in any interval [0,L] is less than the available time; that is, the interval length L. But when a system consists of both periodic task set and aperiodic task set, then we need to consider the aperiodic requests in order to verify the schedulability. Finally, the system is in execution and sometimes it is idle. Thus, it is logical to consider the "idle times" in the processor, otherwise, the system may consider idle time as available time and therefore a mistake is raised.

div.head: Performance studies
div.p: Simulations were made to measure MDAS performance against TBS. This performance was measured by computing the average aperiodic response time as a function of the mean aperiodic load. The response times are presented as time units at the processor. These studies present four graphics, where each one is for a defined periodic load in order to analyse what occurs when the periodic load changes.

The simulation task set consisted of ten periodic tasks randomly generated with a defined utilization factor. The period of each periodic task was established as a random variable uniformly distributed in [0,1] and normalized to give the defined periodic utilization factor.

The aperiodic load was varied until 1-U p , and for each aperiodic load with a defined periodic load 1000 simulations were made. The arrival times of the aperiodic tasks were generated according to an exponential distribution, with average value computed to impose to the specific aperiodic load.

The computation times of the aperiodic tasks were generated according to an uniform distribution between [10,100]. The simulations were generated during 500,000 time units, and some results are illustrated in the followings figures.

div.head: Results
div.p: When the periodic load is close to 0, all the servers get similar results. But, when the periodic load is close to 1, then all servers get a poor performance.

In figure 4, 5, 6 and 7, MDAS offers lower response times (for aperiodic tasks) than TBS. Nevertheless, when the periodic load is high (0.9), the increasing response times is not constant when the aperiodic load is being increasing like in previous cases. This is because the response times depend on the system load, and in this case, system load is high and does not let to vary the response times as a function of the aperiodic load.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: This paper described a new server for improving the response time for aperiodic tasks in a dynamic hard real-time environment, where tasks are attended according to the EDF scheduling algorithm.

In the simulation results, the MDAS behavior is better than TBS, considering response times in the aperiodic load. MDAS set deadlines to the aperiodic tasks considering not only the periodic load, but considering idle times, and that the assignment is still done when there are one or more aperiodic task to execute (aperiodic load). Based on this background, MDAS was proven to be optimal in the sense that minimizes the response time of each aperiodic task,.

The schedulability analysis for aperiodic tasks is not necessary because when deadline is assigned, the analysis is done implicitly (using the processor available time to assign deadlines to the aperiodic tasks).

There exists another proposal in [6] for assigning the best deadline, it is called Improving Total Bandwidth Server (ITBS), so ITBS is equal in performance to MDAS. However the ITBS computational complexity is higher than others algorithms and it was a motivation for working in MDAS. One of our hypotheses is that the MDAS computational complexity is less than the ITBS complexity. In our future research we´ll demonstrate this fact.

Like ITBS, no large memory space is required by the algorithm. In fact, the deadline assignment functions are easier to calculate than the presented in ITBS. The algorithm usage could be attractive when the processor needs are to attend a big amount of aperiodic tasks or when periodic load is high.
